title: Tankas of the Thar
body: In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly in Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost every house traditionally had an underground tank, or tanka, for storing drinking water. The tankas were part of a well-developed rooftop rainwater harvesting system and were built inside the main house or the courtyard. A pipe connected each tanka to the sloping roof of the house, so that rain falling on the roof travelled down the pipe into the tank. The first spell of rain was usually not collected, since it cleaned the roofs and pipes; water from later showers was stored. A tank could be as large as a big room: one household in Phalodi had a tank 6.1 metres deep, 4.27 metres long and 2.44 metres wide. The stored rainwater, called palar pani, lasted till the next rainfall and was a reliable source of drinking water in summer.

title: Rain-rich Gendathur
body: Gendathur is a remote, backward village in Mysuru, Karnataka. Its villagers have installed rooftop rainwater harvesting systems on their houses to meet their water needs. Nearly 200 households have installed the system, and the village has earned the rare distinction of being rich in rainwater. Gendathur receives an annual precipitation of about 1,000 mm. With about 80 per cent collection efficiency and about 10 fillings of the storage, every house can collect and use about 50,000 litres of water in a year.
